}) }

OperationRetries bounds how long the client keeps retrying an operation a server has not accepted, which is unbounded by default. A server sometimes answers "not now": a broker is still starting, a topic is moving between brokers, a subscription is taken. The client then tries again, by default for ever and five seconds apart. That is what waits out a broker restart. attempts(n) gives up after n tries and reports what the server answered. One try makes the first answer final. delay sets the wait between tries, five seconds by default, and timeout the time one try has to be answered, thirty seconds by default. PulsarBroker::operation_retries applies the bound. The bound covers every retried operation of the connection: topic lookups, opening producers and consumers, and a consumer's reconnect after a disconnect. A short bound turns a long outage into a subscription that gives up. The case that needs a bound is an Exclusive subscription another consumer holds. Unbounded, the second consumer waits for the first to leave, and the service does not start. Bounded, startup fails with PulsarError::Subscribe, naming the topic. In a TestApp test the in-process transport refuses a second Exclusive consumer at once, so the bound shows only against a server. Connecting to a production cluster bounds the retries of a service and tests the configuration.

The ledger has one writer at a time. A second instance of the service tries three times, a second apart, and then fails its startup instead of waiting. Macros Manual examples/pulsar_broker_retries.rs /// The cluster at `url`; an operation the server keeps refusing fails after three tries. fn broker(url: &str) -> PulsarBroker { PulsarBroker::new(url) .operation_retries(OperationRetries::attempts(nonzero!(3u32)).delay(Duration::from_secs(1))) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(broker("pulsar://localhost:6650")) } examples/manual/pulsar_broker_retries.rs /// The cluster at `url`; an operation the server keeps refusing fails after three tries. fn broker(url: &str) -> PulsarBroker { PulsarBroker::new(url) .operation_retries(OperationRetries::attempts(nonzero!(3u32)).delay(Duration::from_secs(1))) } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(broker("pulsar://localhost:6650"), ledger("ledger")) }

One glob, ruststream_pulsar::prelude, brings the core prelude, the broker, its descriptor, positions, context keys and Publish. use ruststream_pulsar::prelude::*; is the one import a Pulsar routes file writes. It carries the core's own prelude, so #[subscriber], RustStream, HandlerOutcome and Out come with it. It adds PulsarBroker and OperationRetries, the descriptor PulsarSubscription with SubscriptionType and PulsarTopic, the positions PulsarPosition and PulsarSeeker, and the context types with their keys Position and SeekHandle. The core traits Positioned and Seeker come with them. The publish policy comes under the name every broker crate uses: Publish is PulsarPublish. So a mount site reads the same on every broker. Two broker preludes in one file collide on this name; the prefixed type at the crate root tells them apart. A handler body bounds its slots with capability traits, such as Out<impl Publisher>, and names no broker type. The one exception is a body that keys a publish: partition_key needs PulsarPublishSteps in scope and the slot bounded Out<impl Publisher<Options = PulsarPublishOptions>, Marker>, both from this prelude.

The descriptor, its subscription type, the broker's retries and the reply policy all come from the one glob. Macros Manual examples/pulsar_broker_prelude.rs use ruststream_pulsar::prelude::*; #[subscriber( PulsarSubscription::new("orders", "confirmations-svc") .subscription_type(SubscriptionType::KeyShared), reply )] async fn confirm(order: &Order) -> Confirmation { Confirmation { id: order.id } } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { let broker = PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650") .operation_retries(OperationRetries::attempts(nonzero!(5u32))); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(confirm).out_reply(Publish); }) } examples/manual/pulsar_broker_prelude.rs use ruststream_pulsar::prelude::*; struct Confirm; impl Handle<Order, Confirmation> for Confirm { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Confirmation, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(Confirmation { id: order.id })) } } fn app() -> impl App { let broker = PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650") .operation_retries(OperationRetries::attempts(nonzero!(5u32))); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include( subscriber( PulsarSubscription::new("orders", "confirmations-svc") .subscription_type(SubscriptionType::KeyShared), Confirm, ) .reply() .build(), ) .out_reply(Publish); }) }

token attaches a JWT to the connection, pulsar+ssl:// dials the TLS listener, and credentials never reach the generated document. token is Pulsar's token authentication: the client sends the JWT when it connects and when it reconnects. A service reads the token from its environment or its secret store, as the example does. A pulsar+ssl:// URL dials the server's TLS listener, port 6651 by convention. The client verifies the server's certificate against the system's trusted roots and checks its host name. The connection is TLS from the first byte, so the URL is the whole setting. A TestApp test runs the same broker in process. It checks the URL as the client parses it, and the token goes nowhere. The generated AsyncAPI document reports the host and the port, and never the token or a user name in the URL. Connecting to a production cluster takes the service URL and the token from the environment.

The service authenticates with the token in PULSAR_TOKEN and talks to the cluster over TLS. Macros Manual examples/pulsar_broker_security.rs /// The cluster's TLS listener, authenticated with a JWT. fn broker(token: &str) -> PulsarBroker { PulsarBroker::new("pulsar+ssl://pulsar.acme.internal:6651").token(token) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { let token = env::var("PULSAR_TOKEN").unwrap_or_default(); service(broker(&token)) } examples/manual/pulsar_broker_security.rs /// The cluster's TLS listener, authenticated with a JWT. fn broker(token: &str) -> PulsarBroker { PulsarBroker::new("pulsar+ssl://pulsar.acme.internal:6651").token(token) } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { let token = env::var("PULSAR_TOKEN").unwrap_or_default(); service(broker(&token)) }

Shutdown closes the producers the crate opened, and a publisher or a seek used afterwards reports PulsarError::NotConnected. The crate opens one producer per topic the service publishes to, on the first publish there. At shutdown it closes each of them, so the server releases them at once. A producer that fails to close is logged and does not fail the shutdown. The client's connection itself ends with the client. The shutdown therefore returns (), with no report of its own. A publisher taken before the shutdown keeps pointing at the closed connection. That includes one taken off the broker before startup with PulsarBroker::publisher. A publish through it returns PulsarError::NotConnected and never succeeds against the dead connection. A seek through a handle that outlived the connection is refused the same way.

The service replies to each order with a shipment, which opens a producer on shipments; shutdown closes it. Macros Manual examples/pulsar_broker_shutdown.rs /// The service on `broker`. Its replies open a producer on `shipments`, which shutdown closes. fn service(broker: PulsarBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shipping", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(ship).out_reply(Publish); }) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650")) } examples/manual/pulsar_broker_shutdown.rs /// The service on `broker`. Its replies open a producer on `shipments`, which shutdown closes. fn service(broker: PulsarBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shipping", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include( subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("orders", "shipping"), Ship) .reply() .build(), ) .out_reply(Publish); }) } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650")) }

At startup the runtime dials the service URL, then opens a consumer per subscription; a refused descriptor stops the start. The connect builds the client and dials the URL once. A URL the client cannot parse fails it with PulsarError::Connect. Each subscription then opens its consumer over that connection. Before any I/O, the crate checks what needs no server and refuses it with PulsarError::Invalid: an empty subscription name or an empty topic list; a topic name Pulsar does not accept; a pattern that is not a regular expression; a retry cap without a dead-letter topic, or the reverse, and a cap on an Exclusive or Failover subscription (see Dead letters); a bare topic name on a broker with no default subscription; the error names that setting. A consumer the server refuses fails with PulsarError::Subscribe, naming the topic. A second consumer of an Exclusive subscription waits for the first to leave, unless OperationRetries bounds the tries. One refused subscription fails the whole startup, and the service exits before it reads anything. A TestApp test refuses the same descriptors, so a service that does not start in production does not start in its tests either.

The service reads orders by its bare name, in the default subscription orders-svc, and every audit-* topic through a pattern. Macros Manual examples/pulsar_broker_startup.rs /// A bare topic name: it joins the broker's default subscription. #[subscriber("orders")] async fn place(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// A pattern: checked as a regular expression before its consumer opens. #[subscriber(PulsarSubscription::pattern("audit-.*", "auditors"))] async fn audit(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order audited"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn service(broker: PulsarBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(place); b.include(audit); }) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650").default_subscription("orders-svc")) } examples/manual/pulsar_broker_startup.rs struct Place; impl Handle<Order> for Place { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); ready(Ok(())) } } struct Audit; impl Handle<Order> for Audit { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order audited"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn service(broker: PulsarBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // A bare topic name: it joins the broker's default subscription. b.include(subscriber("orders", Place).build()); // A pattern: checked as a regular expression before its consumer opens. b.include(subscriber(PulsarSubscription::pattern("audit-.*", "auditors"), Audit).build()); }) } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650").default_subscription("orders-svc")) }

PulsarContext gives a handler where its delivery sits in the log and the handle that moves the subscription, each read through Ctx. The subscription builds it once per delivery, beside the payload and the headers, with no allocation. A handler binds one field with Ctx<K>, where K is a key: Key Value What it is Position PulsarPosition the delivery's message id; a seek to it delivers this message again SeekHandle PulsarSeeker the handle that moves the subscription, on every topic it reads Both keys are in the prelude. Ctx<Position> copies the message id, while ctx.context(Position) borrows it. A body that reads both keys takes ctx: &mut Context<'_, PulsarContext> instead and calls ctx.context(key) per key. In the manual form the context is the fourth parameter of Handle: impl Handle<Job, (), (), PulsarContext>. A batch body reads a PulsarBatchContext, which carries the seek handle alone. Replay and seeking reads the seek handle from the context to index every order again.

A job whose result was lost moves the subscription back to its own position, so it is done again. Macros Manual examples/pulsar_context.rs /// Logs where each job sits; a job whose result was lost moves the subscription back to its /// own position, so the job is delivered again. #[subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("jobs", "workers"))] async fn work( job: &Job, ctx: &mut Context<'_, PulsarContext>, State(redos): State<Arc<Redos>>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(job.id, at = ?ctx.context(Position), "job done"); if job.redo && redos.first_time(job) { let at = ctx.context(Position).clone(); if ctx.context(SeekHandle).seek(at).await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/pulsar_context.rs /// Logs where each job sits; a job whose result was lost moves the subscription back to its /// own position, so the job is delivered again. struct Work; impl Handle<Job, (), (), PulsarContext, AppState> for Work { async fn handle( &self, job: &Job, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, PulsarContext, AppState>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { tracing::info!(job.id, at = ?ctx.context(Position), "job done"); if job.redo && ctx.state().redos.first_time(job) { let at = ctx.context(Position).clone(); if ctx.context(SeekHandle).seek(at).await.is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } } Ok(()) } }

A batch handler's context, PulsarBatchContext, carries the subscription's seek handle alone; asking a batch for Position does not compile. A batch spans many deliveries, so it has no single position in the log. The subscription builds the context once per batch, from what every delivery of the batch shares: the SeekHandle key, the same key a PulsarContext carries. A batch body takes ctx: &mut Context<'_, PulsarBatchContext> and reads the handle with ctx.context(SeekHandle). A seek from a batch body takes effect once the batch has settled, so the next batch opens at the new position. Position is a compile error in a batch body, because the batch context does not carry it. In the manual form the context is the fourth parameter of Handle: impl Handle<[Job], (), (), PulsarBatchContext>.

A batch that holds a job whose result was lost replays the retained log once. Macros Manual examples/pulsar_context.rs /// A batch with a job whose result was lost settles first; the seek then replays the /// retained log, so the next batch opens at the beginning. #[subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("jobs", "bulk"))] async fn work( jobs: &[Job], ctx: &mut Context<'_, PulsarBatchContext>, State(redos): State<Arc<Redos>>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(count = jobs.len(), "jobs done"); let redo = jobs.iter().any(|job| job.redo && redos.first_time(job)); if redo && ctx .context(SeekHandle) .seek(PulsarPosition::earliest()) .await .is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/pulsar_context.rs /// A batch with a job whose result was lost settles first; the seek then replays the /// retained log, so the next batch opens at the beginning. struct Work; impl Handle<[Job], (), (), PulsarBatchContext, AppState> for Work { async fn handle( &self, jobs: &[Job], _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, PulsarBatchContext, AppState>, ) -> Result<(), Vec<HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(count = jobs.len(), "jobs done"); let redos = &ctx.state().redos; let redo = jobs.iter().any(|job| job.redo && redos.first_time(job)); if redo && ctx .context(SeekHandle) .seek(PulsarPosition::earliest()) .await .is_err() { return Err(jobs.iter().map(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry()).collect()); } Ok(()) } }

PulsarPosition names a place in a topic's retained log: either end, a delivered message, or a publish time. Pulsar keeps a topic's messages as a log, so a subscription can be moved through it, at startup with start_at or from a handler with a seek. PulsarPosition::earliest() is the oldest message the topic still retains, and every retained message is delivered again from there. PulsarPosition::latest() is the tip of the log: only messages published after the move are delivered. PulsarPosition::timestamp(millis) is the first message published at or after that time, in milliseconds since the Unix epoch. A delivery's own place is a position as well: Ctx<Position> binds it through the Position key, a copy the handler can keep. A seek to such a position delivers that message again, then the rest of the log in order. A position applies to every topic and every partition the subscription reads. A non-persistent topic retains nothing, so a move over it replays nothing. Replay and seeking rebuilds balances from a ledger on every startup and indexes every order again with a seek.

A projection bookmarks the entry that closes a day; a rebuild request moves the ledger subscription back to it. Macros Manual examples/pulsar_positions.rs /// Where the projection last closed a day: the ledger subscription's seeker and the position /// of the entry that closed it. #[derive(Clone, Default)] struct Bookmark(Arc<Mutex<Option<(PulsarSeeker, PulsarPosition)>>>); #[derive(FromRef)] struct AppState { bookmark: Bookmark, } /// Projects each ledger entry and bookmarks the entry that closes a day. #[subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("ledger", "projection"))] async fn project( entry: &Entry, Ctx(position): Ctx<Position>, Ctx(seeker): Ctx<SeekHandle>, State(bookmark): State<Bookmark>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(entry.id, "projected"); if entry.closes_day { *bookmark.0.lock().await = Some((seeker, position)); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// Replays the ledger from the last closed day: the entry at the bookmark comes again, then /// every entry after it, in order. #[subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("ledger.rebuild", "projection"))] async fn rebuild(request: &Rebuild, State(bookmark): State<Bookmark>) -> HandlerOutcome { let Some((seeker, position)) = bookmark.0.lock().await.clone() else { return HandlerOutcome::ack(); }; tracing::info!(reason = %request.reason, "rebuilding from the last closed day"); match seeker.seek(position).await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(err) => { tracing::warn!(%err, "the ledger cannot be rewound"); HandlerOutcome::retry() } } } examples/manual/pulsar_positions.rs /// Where the projection last closed a day: the ledger subscription's seeker and the position /// of the entry that closed it. #[derive(Clone, Default)] struct Bookmark(Arc<Mutex<Option<(PulsarSeeker, PulsarPosition)>>>); struct AppState { bookmark: Bookmark, } /// Projects each ledger entry and bookmarks the entry that closes a day. struct Project; impl Handle<Entry, (), (), PulsarContext, AppState> for Project { async fn handle( &self, entry: &Entry, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, PulsarContext, AppState>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { tracing::info!(entry.id, "projected"); if entry.closes_day { let mark = ( ctx.context(SeekHandle).clone(), ctx.context(Position).clone(), ); *ctx.state().bookmark.0.lock().await = Some(mark); } Ok(()) } } /// Replays the ledger from the last closed day: the entry at the bookmark comes again, then /// every entry after it, in order. struct Rewind; impl Handle<Rebuild, (), (), PulsarContext, AppState> for Rewind { async fn handle( &self, request: &Rebuild, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, PulsarContext, AppState>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let Some((seeker, position)) = ctx.state().bookmark.0.lock().await.clone() else { return Ok(()); }; tracing::info!(reason = %request.reason, "rebuilding from the last closed day"); seeker.seek(position).await.map_err(|err| { tracing::warn!(%err, "the ledger cannot be rewound"); HandlerOutcome::retry() }) } } fn app() -> impl App<State = AppState> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("ledger", "0.1.0")) .on_startup(async move |()| { Ok::<_, Infallible>(AppState { bookmark: Bookmark::default(), }) }) .with_broker(PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650"), |b| { b.include(subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("ledger", "projection"), Project).build()); b.include( subscriber( PulsarSubscription::new("ledger.rebuild", "projection"), Rewind, ) .build(), ); }) }

A handler moves its whole subscription through the SeekHandle key; queued deliveries are dropped and replay starts at the target. Ctx<SeekHandle> binds a PulsarSeeker for the subscription the delivery came from. Its seek(position) takes a PulsarPosition, and the next delivery comes from there. The seek moves the subscription, not one consumer: every topic and every partition it reads, and every consumer that shares it. Deliveries already queued when the seek lands are dropped, so the handler never sees them. A batch still being assembled is the exception: it closes with the deliveries it had taken. A seeker is a value, so a handler can keep it and move the subscription later from elsewhere, as the PulsarPosition example does. A seek after the service shut down returns PulsarError::NotConnected. A batch handler reaches the same key through its PulsarBatchContext. A position that has to apply on each boot belongs in start_at instead. Replay and seeking indexes every order again with a seek from the handler.

A job marked poisoned starts a run the producer knows to be unprocessable; the subscription jumps to the tip of the log past it. Macros Manual examples/pulsar_positions_seek.rs /// Skips a poisoned run: the subscription jumps to the tip of the log, and the jobs queued /// behind the marker never reach the handler. #[subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("jobs", "workers"))] async fn work(job: &Job, Ctx(seeker): Ctx<SeekHandle>) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(job.id, "worked"); if !job.poisoned { return HandlerOutcome::ack(); } match seeker.seek(PulsarPosition::latest()).await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(err) => { tracing::warn!(job.id, %err, "the poisoned run cannot be skipped"); HandlerOutcome::retry() } } } examples/manual/pulsar_positions_seek.rs /// Skips a poisoned run: the subscription jumps to the tip of the log, and the jobs queued /// behind the marker never reach the handler. struct Work; impl Handle<Job, (), (), PulsarContext> for Work { async fn handle( &self, job: &Job, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, PulsarContext>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { tracing::info!(job.id, "worked"); if !job.poisoned { return Ok(()); } ctx.context(SeekHandle) .seek(PulsarPosition::latest()) .await .map_err(|err| { tracing::warn!(job.id, %err, "the poisoned run cannot be skipped"); HandlerOutcome::retry() }) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("jobs", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650"), |b| { b.include(subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("jobs", "workers"), Work).build()); }, ) }

start_at seeks a subscription to a position on every startup, rewinding its durable cursor, unlike Pulsar's initial position. It is a clause of the attribute, start_at(PulsarPosition::earliest()), or .start_at(position) among the mount-site settings. A Pulsar subscription is durable state on the broker: its cursor records what was acknowledged, and it outlives the service. The seek lands before the subscription's first delivery, so the handler sees the log from the position on. start_at(PulsarPosition::earliest()) therefore replays the retained backlog each time the service starts, acknowledged messages included. Pulsar's own initial position is different: the broker applies it only when it creates the subscription. A subscription without the clause resumes from its cursor. It suits a read model rebuilt from the retained log on each boot. Replay and seeking rebuilds account balances from a ledger on every startup.

The audit projection is rebuilt from the oldest retained entry on every startup, although its subscription acknowledged everything it read before. Macros Manual examples/pulsar_positions_start_at.rs /// Rebuilds the audit projection from the oldest retained entry on every startup. #[subscriber( PulsarSubscription::new("ledger.audit", "audit"), start_at(PulsarPosition::earliest()) )] async fn replay(entry: &AuditEntry) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(entry.id, "projected"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/pulsar_positions_start_at.rs /// Projects every audit entry it reads. struct Replay; impl Handle<AuditEntry> for Replay { fn handle( &self, entry: &AuditEntry, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(entry.id, "projected"); ready(Ok(())) } } /// The service on the Pulsar cluster `url` names. fn service(url: &str) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("audit", "0.1.0")).with_broker(PulsarBroker::new(url), |b| { // The projection is rebuilt from the oldest retained entry on every startup. b.include( subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("ledger.audit", "audit"), Replay) .start_at(PulsarPosition::earliest()) .build(), ); }) }

PulsarPublish, Publish in the prelude, opens one producer per topic and waits for the broker's receipt, so Ok means stored. A mount site names it wherever a registration publishes: .out_reply(Publish) for a reply, .out(Slot, Publish) for a slot. The policy holds no connection; the runtime pairs it with the connected broker at startup into a PulsarPublisher. A registration that names no policy for its reply publishes through this one. A reply goes to the topic its type names with #[outgoing(name = "..")], or to the one a reply("..") clause names when the type leaves it open. The publisher opens a producer for a topic on the first publish there and keeps it until shutdown. A publish returns once the broker has stored the message, or with the error it reported. Outside a handler, PulsarBroker::publisher hands out a publisher before the service starts. Per message, a publish carries headers and a key. Publishing and replies confirms orders with receipts and answers price quotes.

Macros Manual examples/pulsar_publishing_publish.rs /// The receipt of an order; the type names the topic it goes to. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "receipts")] struct Receipt { order_id: u64, } /// Confirms each order with a receipt. #[subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("orders", "confirmations"), reply)] async fn confirm(order: &Order) -> Receipt { tracing::info!(order.id, "order confirmed"); Receipt { order_id: order.id } } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650"), |b| { b.include(confirm).out_reply(Publish); }, ) } examples/manual/pulsar_publishing_publish.rs /// The receipt of an order; the type names the topic it goes to. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[outgoing(name = "receipts")] struct Receipt { order_id: u64, } /// Confirms each order with a receipt. struct Confirm; impl Handle<Order, Receipt> for Confirm { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Receipt, HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order confirmed"); ready(Ok(Receipt { order_id: order.id })) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650"), |b| { let confirm = subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("orders", "confirmations"), Confirm); b.include(confirm.reply().build()).out_reply(Publish); }, ) }

A header travels as a Pulsar message property, one per header and no envelope; a value that is not UTF-8 fails the publish. The property has the header's name and value, so a consumer in another language reads it as a plain Pulsar property. The payload stays the encoded message alone. A message type declares its headers in a typed contract, #[outgoing(headers = ..)], and the handler sets them with with_headers. A HeaderMap written by hand works the same. Pulsar properties are text, so a header value that is not valid UTF-8 fails the publish with PulsarError::Publish. On delivery the properties come back as the message's headers. One header has a meaning of its own: the partition-key header becomes the message key. Publishing and replies sends pick lists with headers to warehouses.

Macros Manual examples/pulsar_publishing_headers.rs /// The header contract of an invoice: the tenant it belongs to travels as the `tenant` property. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize)] struct Tenant { tenant: String, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "invoices", headers = Tenant)] struct Invoice { order_id: u64, } #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Invoice)] struct Invoices; /// Issues the invoice of each order under its tenant. #[subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("orders", "billing"))] async fn issue(order: &Order, Out(invoices): Out<impl Publisher, Invoices>) -> HandlerOutcome { let tenant = Tenant { tenant: order.tenant.clone(), }; let sent = invoices .message(&Invoice { order_id: order.id }) .with_headers(&tenant) .publish() .await; match sent { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(err) => { tracing::warn!(order.id, %err, "the invoice was not issued"); HandlerOutcome::retry() } } } examples/manual/pulsar_publishing_headers.rs /// The header contract of an invoice: the tenant it belongs to travels as the `tenant` property. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema)] struct Tenant { tenant: String, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[outgoing(name = "invoices", headers = Tenant)] struct Invoice { order_id: u64, } #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Invoice)] struct Invoices; /// Issues the invoice of each order under its tenant. struct Issue; impl<Entry> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Issue where Entry: OutEntry<Invoices, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let tenant = Tenant { tenant: order.tenant.clone(), }; outs.get(Invoices) .message(&Invoice { order_id: order.id }) .with_headers(&tenant) .publish() .await .map_err(|err| { tracing::warn!(order.id, %err, "the invoice was not issued"); HandlerOutcome::retry() }) } }

The partition-key header, PARTITION_KEY_HEADER, is the message key: it picks the partition of a partitioned topic and orders KeyShared and by_key lanes. The header is named partition-key. On publish its value becomes the Pulsar message key and does not travel as a property of its own. On a partitioned topic the producer hashes the key, so every message of one key goes to one partition, in the order it was published. A publish without a key spreads over the partitions in turn. A message type declares the header in its typed contract, #[outgoing(headers = ..)], with a field renamed to partition-key; a HeaderMap with that entry works the same. On consume the key comes back as that header. A KeyShared subscription hands every message of one key to one consumer, and workers(n, by_key) keeps one key on one lane inside a consumer. A handler body that keys one publish of a slot uses the partition_key step instead. Subscription types and ordering places keyed messages on the partitions of a partitioned topic.

Macros Manual examples/pulsar_publishing_keys.rs /// The header a shipment carries: `partition-key`, which becomes the message key. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize)] struct ShipmentKey { #[serde(rename = "partition-key")] customer: String, } /// Every shipment of one customer carries one key, so the partition and the consumer that /// take it see that customer's shipments in order. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "shipments", headers = ShipmentKey)] struct Shipment { order_id: u64, } #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Shipment)] struct Shipments; #[subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("orders", "shipping"))] async fn ship(order: &Order, Out(shipments): Out<impl Publisher, Shipments>) -> HandlerOutcome { let key = ShipmentKey { customer: order.customer.clone(), }; let shipment = Shipment { order_id: order.id }; if shipments .message(&shipment) .with_headers(&key) .publish() .await .is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/pulsar_publishing_keys.rs /// The header a shipment carries: `partition-key`, which becomes the message key. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema)] struct ShipmentKey { #[serde(rename = "partition-key")] customer: String, } /// Every shipment of one customer carries one key, so the partition and the consumer that /// take it see that customer's shipments in order. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[outgoing(name = "shipments", headers = ShipmentKey)] struct Shipment { order_id: u64, } #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Shipment)] struct Shipments; struct Ship; impl<Entry> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Ship where Entry: OutEntry<Shipments, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let key = ShipmentKey { customer: order.customer.clone(), }; let shipment = Shipment { order_id: order.id }; outs.get(Shipments) .message(&shipment) .with_headers(&key) .publish() .await .map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry()) } }

The partition_key step keys one publish from a handler body; it wins over a partition-key header and keeps the slot's codec. The key does what the partition-key header does: it places the message on a partition and orders KeyShared consumers. The step writes the one field of PulsarPublishOptions and returns the builder. The message still leaves through the slot the mount site wired, in that slot's codec and through its transforms. A body reaches the step by bounding its slot Out<impl Publisher<Options = PulsarPublishOptions>, Slot>. That body imports ruststream_pulsar::prelude::*, the one case where a handler body names this broker. The mount site declares nothing for it, and a publish without the step goes unkeyed. Where a publish carries both the step and the header, the step wins. A test reads the key a slot publish carried with tb.out::<Slot>().with_options(..). Publishing and replies keys each pick list by its warehouse.

Macros Manual examples/pulsar_publishing_partition_key.rs /// Records a receipt per order, keyed by the user who placed it, so one user's receipts stay /// in order. A body that names a per-message setting imports this broker's prelude and states /// the settings type on its slot. #[subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("orders", "ledger"))] async fn record( order: &Order, Out(ledger): Out<impl Publisher<Options = PulsarPublishOptions>, Ledger>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { let sent = ledger .message(&Receipt { order_id: order.id }) .partition_key(format!("user-{}", order.user)) .publish() .await; match sent { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(err) => { tracing::warn!(order.id, %err, "the receipt was not recorded"); HandlerOutcome::retry() } } } examples/manual/pulsar_publishing_partition_key.rs /// Records a receipt per order, keyed by the user who placed it, so one user's receipts stay /// in order. struct Record; impl<Entry> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Record where Entry: OutEntry<Ledger, Wire: Publisher<Options = PulsarPublishOptions>>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { outs.get(Ledger) .message(&Receipt { order_id: order.id }) .partition_key(format!("user-{}", order.user)) .publish() .await .map_err(|err| { tracing::warn!(order.id, %err, "the receipt was not recorded"); HandlerOutcome::retry() }) } }

ack acknowledges a Pulsar delivery, retry negatively acknowledges it, and drop acknowledges it too: Pulsar has no terminal reject. The handler's outcome settles each delivery on its subscription. An acknowledged message moves the subscription's cursor past it, and the subscription does not deliver it again. A negative acknowledgement hands the message back to the subscription, not to the consumer that gave up on it: on a Shared subscription another consumer may take it. A message that should leave the subscription for good goes through a dead-letter policy, which drop does not need. The client queues acknowledgements and sends them in the background, so a settlement that returns is queued on the consumer, not yet confirmed by the broker. A message nobody settles comes back after the subscription's ack_timeout. retry_after asks for the delivery back after a delay. Acknowledgement settles the stock reservations of an inventory service by the handler's outcome.

Macros Manual examples/pulsar_settlement_ack.rs /// Reserves the stock of each order. `ack` acknowledges the message; `retry` negatively /// acknowledges it and the subscription delivers it again; `drop` acknowledges it as well, so an /// order of nothing is never seen again. #[subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("orders", "fulfilment"))] async fn fulfil(order: &Order, State(warehouse): State<Warehouse>) -> HandlerOutcome { if order.quantity == 0 { tracing::warn!(order.id, "an order of nothing is dropped"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } match warehouse.reserve(order).await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(err) => { tracing::warn!(order.id, %err, "reservation failed, redelivering"); HandlerOutcome::retry() } } } examples/manual/pulsar_settlement_ack.rs /// Reserves the stock of each order. `Ok` acknowledges the message; `Err(retry)` negatively /// acknowledges it and the subscription delivers it again; `Err(drop)` acknowledges it as well, /// so an order of nothing is never seen again. struct Fulfil; impl Handle<Order, (), (), (), AppState> for Fulfil { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), AppState>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { if order.quantity == 0 { tracing::warn!(order.id, "an order of nothing is dropped"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); } ctx.state().warehouse.reserve(order).await.map_err(|err| { tracing::warn!(order.id, %err, "reservation failed, redelivering"); HandlerOutcome::retry() }) } }

ack_timeout redelivers a message left unacknowledged longer than the timeout; it also bounds the delay a retry_after may ask for. It is a setting of the PulsarSubscription descriptor and has no default: without it, an unsettled message comes back only when its consumer disconnects. With it, the client asks the broker for every message its handler has held longer than the timeout, whatever the reason: a handler that hangs, or a service that stopped mid-delivery. Each such redelivery counts toward the dead-letter cap, as a retry does. A retry_after delay that is not shorter than the timeout is refused when the handler returns it, with an error naming both values, because the timeout would bring the message back first. A handler keeps its backoff below the timeout for that reason. The in-process transport of a TestApp test applies the bound on retry_after; the redelivery itself happens on a broker. Acknowledgement bounds an unsettled delivery of an inventory service with an acknowledgement timeout.

An export the archive refused waits thirty seconds, inside the one-minute ack timeout of its subscription. Macros Manual examples/pulsar_settlement_ack_timeout.rs /// How long the archive gets before the next upload: shorter than the ack timeout, which would /// bring the export back first. const BACKOFF: Duration = Duration::from_secs(30); /// Uploads each export. An export nobody settles within a minute, because the handler hangs or /// the service stops, comes back from the broker. #[subscriber( PulsarSubscription::new("exports", "archiver").ack_timeout(Duration::from_secs(60)) )] async fn upload(export: &Export, State(archive): State<Archive>) -> HandlerOutcome { match archive.upload(export).await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(err) => { tracing::warn!(export.id, %err, "upload failed, trying again later"); HandlerOutcome::retry_after(BACKOFF) } } } examples/manual/pulsar_settlement_ack_timeout.rs /// How long the archive gets before the next upload: shorter than the ack timeout, which would /// bring the export back first. const BACKOFF: Duration = Duration::from_secs(30); /// Uploads each export. struct Upload; impl Handle<Export, (), (), (), AppState> for Upload { async fn handle( &self, export: &Export, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), AppState>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { ctx.state().archive.upload(export).await.map_err(|err| { tracing::warn!(export.id, %err, "upload failed, trying again later"); HandlerOutcome::retry_after(BACKOFF) }) } } fn app() -> impl App<State = AppState> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("archiver", "0.1.0")) .on_startup(async move |()| { Ok::<_, Infallible>(AppState { archive: Archive::default(), }) }) .with_broker(PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650"), |b| { // An export nobody settles within a minute, because the handler hangs or the service // stops, comes back from the broker. b.include( subscriber( PulsarSubscription::new("exports", "archiver") .ack_timeout(Duration::from_secs(60)), Upload, ) .build(), ); }) }

max_attempts with dead_letter becomes the consumer's own dead-letter policy: the client moves a spent message, and the service publishes nothing. max_attempts(n) is how many times one message reaches the handler, the first delivery included. dead_letter(topic) is where it goes once those are spent. The Pulsar client counts the redeliveries, produces the spent message to that topic and acknowledges the original. A retry, a retry_after and an expired ack_timeout each advance the count. The two steps go together: a registration that writes one without the other refuses to start, and the error names the missing step. The broker counts redeliveries only where consumers compete for messages, so the cap belongs to a Shared or a KeyShared subscription. A registration that declares a cap over Exclusive or Failover refuses to start, and the error names the type. A handler mounted by a bare topic name declares the same pair, and one policy covers every topic of a multi-topic subscription. The client keeps the count to itself, so a handler cannot read how many deliveries a message has had. Retries and dead letters caps the deliveries of a refunds service and reads its dead letters.

Macros Manual examples/pulsar_settlement_dead_letters.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("bookkeeping", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650"), |b| { // Three deliveries in all; then the client moves the payment to `payments-dlq`. b.include(book) .max_attempts(nonzero!(3)) .dead_letter("payments-dlq"); }, ) } examples/manual/pulsar_settlement_dead_letters.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("bookkeeping", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650"), |b| { // Three deliveries in all; then the client moves the payment to `payments-dlq`. b.include(subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("payments", "bookkeeping"), Book).build()) .max_attempts(nonzero!(3)) .dead_letter("payments-dlq"); }, ) }

retry_after(delay) holds the delivery unacknowledged in the service for the delay, then negatively acknowledges it; nothing is republished. A Pulsar negative acknowledgement carries no delay of its own, so the wait happens in the service. When it is over, the subscription delivers the same message again, with its own payload, properties and position. The redelivery is an ordinary one, so a dead-letter policy counts it like any other. The wait runs on the runtime the broker connected on. A process that exits during the wait loses the wait, not the message: the broker delivers it again once the ack_timeout elapses, or at once when the consumer disconnects. A delay that is not shorter than the subscription's ack_timeout is refused when the handler returns it; a subscription with no ack_timeout accepts any delay. A test waits the delay out with tb.advance, in process on a paused clock and against a live broker in real time. Retries and dead letters holds a refund back while the card processor's rate limit is used up.

An invoice whose customer has not reached the directory yet comes back after the replication lag. Macros Manual examples/pulsar_settlement_retry_after.rs /// How long a customer the directory has not replicated yet gets before the next try. const REPLICATION_LAG: Duration = Duration::from_secs(2); /// Issues each invoice. An invoice whose customer is missing waits in the service for the lag, /// then the broker delivers it again. #[subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("invoices", "billing"))] async fn issue(invoice: &Invoice, State(directory): State<Directory>) -> HandlerOutcome { match directory.find(invoice.customer).await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(err) => { tracing::warn!(invoice.id, %err, "customer not found, trying again later"); HandlerOutcome::retry_after(REPLICATION_LAG) } } } examples/manual/pulsar_settlement_retry_after.rs /// How long a customer the directory has not replicated yet gets before the next try. const REPLICATION_LAG: Duration = Duration::from_secs(2); /// Issues each invoice. An invoice whose customer is missing waits in the service for the lag, /// then the broker delivers it again. struct Issue; impl Handle<Invoice, (), (), (), AppState> for Issue { async fn handle( &self, invoice: &Invoice, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), AppState>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { ctx.state() .directory .find(invoice.customer) .await .map_err(|err| { tracing::warn!(invoice.id, %err, "customer not found, trying again later"); HandlerOutcome::retry_after(REPLICATION_LAG) }) } }

A topic in #[subscriber] joins the broker's default subscription on it; a PulsarSubscription carries every other setting. #[subscriber("orders")] reads the topic orders, which is persistent://public/default/orders. Pulsar reads a topic only through a named subscription, and a bare name names none, so the name comes from PulsarBroker::default_subscription. A bare name on a broker with no default subscription stops the service at startup with an error that names the setting. The subscription is a durable cursor on the server, and it is Shared: every handler and every instance of a service that joins it competes for its messages. Name it after the service that owns the cursor, because another service that names the same subscription shares its backlog. Every other setting of a subscription belongs to a descriptor, which goes where the name goes, as the attribute's first argument: Descriptor Reads PulsarSubscription::new one topic PulsarSubscription::topics a fixed list of topics PulsarSubscription::pattern every topic whose name matches a regular expression The manual form passes the name or the descriptor to subscriber(source, body). A subscription the service creates starts at the tip of its topics, and one that already exists resumes at its cursor; start_at moves it. The Pulsar client moves a delivery whose retries are spent to a dead-letter topic itself, so a registration on any of these forms declares its retries and publishes nothing. Topics and subscriptions builds a fulfilment service on one topic, a fixed list, a pattern and the short form.

The topic orders, read under the subscription orders-svc. Macros Manual examples/pulsar_subscriptions_name.rs /// Reads the topic `orders`; the subscription comes from the broker. #[subscriber("orders")] async fn place(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn app() -> impl App { let broker = PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650").default_subscription("orders-svc"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(place); }) } examples/manual/pulsar_subscriptions_name.rs /// Reads the topic `orders`; the subscription comes from the broker. struct Place; impl Handle<Order> for Place { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { let broker = PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650").default_subscription("orders-svc"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Place).build()); }) }

A slice handler takes a batch the service assembles: full at the mount site's size, or closed batch_wait after its first delivery. A handler over &[T] is a batch handler, and batch(n) at the mount site is its largest batch. The Pulsar client hands over one delivery at a time, so the batch is assembled in the service. A batch closes when it holds n deliveries, or when batch_wait has passed since its first delivery, whichever comes first. batch_wait is a setting of the descriptor, 10 ms by default; a longer wait gives fuller batches on a quiet topic, at the cost of latency. An idle subscription waits for the first delivery as long as it takes, so a batch is never empty. One outcome settles every delivery of the batch. A Vec<HandlerOutcome> settles delivery i with outcome i. workers(n) keeps up to n batches in flight at once. A batch body reads a PulsarBatchContext, which carries the seek handle and no per-delivery field. In the manual form the body is an impl Handle<[T]>, where Ok(()) acks the batch and Err(outcomes) settles delivery by delivery. Acknowledgement records the stock counts of warehouse scans in batches.

Readings that arrive together are stored in one call. Macros Manual examples/pulsar_batches.rs /// Stores a batch of readings in one round-trip; one outcome settles the whole batch. A batch /// that is not full closes 250 ms after its first reading. #[subscriber( PulsarSubscription::new("readings", "aggregator") .batch_wait(Duration::from_millis(250)) )] async fn aggregate(readings: &[Reading]) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(count = readings.len(), "stored in one round-trip"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/pulsar_batches.rs /// Stores a batch of readings in one round-trip; `Ok` settles the whole batch. struct Aggregate; impl Handle<[Reading]> for Aggregate { fn handle( &self, readings: &[Reading], _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), Vec<HandlerOutcome>>> { tracing::info!(count = readings.len(), "stored in one round-trip"); ready(Ok(())) } }

The mount site names the size, so the same handler can run with another size in another service. Macros Manual examples/pulsar_batches.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("readings", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650"), |b| { // At most 64 readings per call. b.include(aggregate.batch(nonzero!(64))); }, ) } examples/manual/pulsar_batches.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("readings", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650"), |b| { // At most 64 readings per call; a batch that is not full closes 250 ms after its // first reading. b.include( subscriber( PulsarSubscription::new("readings", "aggregator") .batch_wait(Duration::from_millis(250)), Aggregate, ) .batch(nonzero!(64)) .build(), ); }, ) }

PulsarSubscription::pattern reads every topic whose full name matches a regular expression, topics created later included. The expression is matched against the full name of each topic, so it is written in full: persistent://public/default/orders-.*. The client lists one namespace for it, the one the prefix names: persistent://acme/orders/.* reads acme/orders, and a pattern with no tenant/namespace/ part reads public/default. The client lists the topics again every 30 seconds and joins the subscription to each new match. A topic created after startup is read from the listing that finds it on, and what reached it before that listing is not delivered. A pattern has no single topic to name the subscription by, so it reports under the subscription's own name. The expression is checked at startup, and one that is not a valid regular expression, or whose tenant or namespace is itself a regular expression, stops the service before any call to the server. The settings and their defaults are those of PulsarSubscription, and a seek moves the cursor on every topic the pattern reads. Topics and subscriptions audits every regional order topic, those created later included.

Every orders-* topic is recorded byte for byte, whatever its producer wrote; returns is not. Macros Manual examples/pulsar_pattern.rs /// What the `orders-*` producers write is not one schema, so the payload rides the byte lane: /// `Deserialized` names the bytes without decoding them. #[derive(Deserialized)] struct Record<'a>(&'a [u8]); /// Records every `orders-*` topic of `public/default`, those created after startup included. #[subscriber(PulsarSubscription::pattern("persistent://public/default/orders-.*", "audit"))] async fn audit(record: &Record<'_>) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(bytes = record.0.len(), "order event recorded"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/pulsar_pattern.rs /// What the `orders-*` producers write is not one schema, so the payload rides the byte lane: /// the type is built from the bytes as they arrived, and no codec runs. struct Record<'a>(&'a [u8]); impl Deserialized for Record<'_> { type Output<'a> = Record<'a>; type Error = Infallible; fn from_payload(payload: &[u8]) -> Result<Record<'_>, Infallible> { Ok(Record(payload)) } } impl Input for Record<'_> { type Axis = SoloDeserialized<Record<'static>>; } /// Records each event of those topics. struct Audit; impl Handle<Record<'_>> for Audit { fn handle( &self, record: &Record<'_>, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(bytes = record.0.len(), "order event recorded"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("audit", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650"), |b| { // Every `orders-*` topic of `public/default`, those created after startup included. b.include( subscriber( PulsarSubscription::pattern("persistent://public/default/orders-.*", "audit"), Audit, ) .build(), ); }, ) }

PulsarSubscription::new joins a named durable subscription on one topic: a bare name, tenant/namespace/topic, or a full name. The first argument is the topic, and the second is the subscription. A bare name is a topic of persistent://public/default, a triple is a persistent topic of that tenant and namespace, and a full name such as non-persistent://acme/sales/pings says everything itself. The subscription is the cursor the server keeps for its readers. Every consumer that joins the same subscription shares one backlog, and a second subscription on the same topic reads every message again, from a cursor of its own. subscription() returns the name. Every setting has a default, so the two names are all a descriptor needs: Setting What it does Default subscription_type how the consumers of the subscription share it Shared ack_timeout redelivers what a handler left unsettled longer than this none batch_wait how long a batch that is not full waits for more deliveries 10 ms The subscription reports under its topic, as written: a test reads its deliveries under that name, and the AsyncAPI document reports that channel. A topic name Pulsar would refuse stops the service at startup with an error that names it, before any call to the server; PulsarTopic is the same check as a type. Topics and subscriptions reads one topic under two subscriptions of a fulfilment service.

Billing and shipping read every order of acme/sales/orders, each under a subscription of its own. Macros Manual examples/pulsar_subscriptions_descriptor.rs /// Bills every order of the `acme/sales` namespace; the subscription `billing` is its cursor. #[subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("acme/sales/orders", "billing"))] async fn bill(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order billed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// Ships the same orders on a cursor of its own. #[subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("acme/sales/orders", "shipping"))] async fn ship(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order shipped"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn app() -> impl App { let broker = PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(bill); b.include(ship); }) } examples/manual/pulsar_subscriptions_descriptor.rs /// Bills every order of the `acme/sales` namespace. struct Bill; impl Handle<Order> for Bill { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order billed"); ready(Ok(())) } } /// Ships the same orders. struct Ship; impl Handle<Order> for Ship { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order shipped"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { let broker = PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // Each subscription is a cursor of its own: `billing` and `shipping` read every order. b.include( subscriber( PulsarSubscription::new("acme/sales/orders", "billing"), Bill, ) .build(), ); b.include( subscriber( PulsarSubscription::new("acme/sales/orders", "shipping"), Ship, ) .build(), ); }) }

PulsarTopic is a topic name checked on construction: persistent and non_persistent for literals, parse for names read at run time. A Pulsar topic name carries four things: the persistence, the tenant, the namespace and the topic. Each of the last three may hold ASCII letters, digits, -, _ and ., and none may be empty. PulsarTopic::persistent and PulsarTopic::non_persistent build a name from its parts and panic on a part Pulsar would refuse, so they are for names written in the code. PulsarTopic::parse is the form for a name that arrives at run time. It accepts a full name, a tenant/namespace/topic triple, which is persistent, or a bare name, which belongs to persistent://public/default, and returns an error for anything else. as_str is the full name, and Display writes the same. persistence, tenant, namespace and name return the parts. A descriptor and a publish parse every topic they are given the same way, so a name Pulsar would refuse never reaches the server: a descriptor stops the service at startup, and a publish returns an error. Topics and subscriptions names the topics of a fulfilment service.

Each order goes to its tenant's own topic; an order naming a tenant that is no valid name part is dropped. Macros Manual examples/pulsar_subscriptions_topic.rs /// The tenants' own order topics. #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Order)] struct TenantOrders; /// Fans orders out to their tenant's topic. The tenant comes off the wire, so its topic is /// parsed, and an order naming a tenant Pulsar would refuse is dropped here. #[subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("orders", "router"))] async fn route(order: &Order, Out(tenants): Out<impl Publisher, TenantOrders>) -> HandlerOutcome { let Ok(topic) = PulsarTopic::parse(&format!("{}/orders/created", order.tenant)) else { tracing::warn!(order.id, tenant = %order.tenant, "no such tenant topic"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); }; match tenants.message(order).to(topic.as_str()).publish().await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(_) => HandlerOutcome::retry(), } } fn app() -> impl App { let broker = PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("router", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(route).out(TenantOrders, Publish).build(); }) } examples/manual/pulsar_subscriptions_topic.rs /// The tenants' own order topics. struct TenantOrders; impl OutSlot for TenantOrders { const NAME: &'static str = "TenantOrders"; type Destination = Reads; } impl PublishedThrough<TenantOrders> for Order {} /// Fans orders out to their tenant's topic. The tenant comes off the wire, so its topic is /// parsed, and an order naming a tenant Pulsar would refuse is dropped here. struct Route; impl<Entry> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Route where Entry: OutEntry<TenantOrders, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let Ok(topic) = PulsarTopic::parse(&format!("{}/orders/created", order.tenant)) else { tracing::warn!(order.id, tenant = %order.tenant, "no such tenant topic"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); }; let tenants = outs.get(TenantOrders); match tenants.message(order).to(topic.as_str()).publish().await { Ok(()) => Ok(()), Err(_) => Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()), } } } fn app() -> impl App { let broker = PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("router", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("orders", "router"), Route).build()) .out(TenantOrders, Publish) .build(); }) }

SubscriptionType says how the consumers of one subscription share it: Exclusive, Shared, Failover or KeyShared. PulsarSubscription::subscription_type sets it, and Shared is the default. Each handler mounted on a subscription is one consumer of it, and so is each instance of the service. A message reaches every subscription on its topic once, and the type decides which consumer of the subscription takes it: Type Who takes a message Exclusive the one consumer of the subscription; a second consumer waits until the first leaves Shared any consumer, in turn Failover the active consumer; a standby takes over when it leaves KeyShared the consumer that holds the message's key, so one key is read in order The server refuses a second Exclusive consumer as busy, and the client asks again until its operation retries run out; with the default retries it asks for ever, so the second instance does not finish starting. An Exclusive subscription belongs to a service that runs one instance. Under the test harness that second consumer is refused at startup instead, so the test fails rather than hangs. A message's key is its partition key. A retry cap needs Shared or KeyShared, because only there does the server count a message's redeliveries; a cap on the other two stops the service at startup, as Dead letters explains. Subscription types and ordering reads a shipping service under each of the four types.

Two workers on the Shared subscription workers: each task runs once, on one of them. PulsarSubscription::topics reads a fixed list of topics under one subscription; one seek or one retry policy covers them all. The first argument is the list, and each topic in it takes any of the three spellings a single topic takes. The subscription keeps a cursor on every topic of the list, and its consumers read all of them. A list has no single topic to name the subscription by, so it reports under the subscription's own name: a test reads its deliveries under that name, and the AsyncAPI document reports that channel. A seek from a handler moves the cursor on every topic of the list. The registration's dead-letter topic is one for the whole list. The settings and their defaults are those of PulsarSubscription. An empty list, or a name in it that Pulsar would refuse, stops the service at startup. Topics and subscriptions totals the orders of two regional topics under one subscription.

The European and the American orders, fulfilled under one subscription. TestApp::start connects PulsarBroker in process: topics, the four subscription types, dead letters, delayed retries and seeking. A test hands the harness the app main runs, unchanged, and addresses the broker by its production type, tb.broker::<PulsarBroker>(). The testing feature in [dev-dependencies] adds the in-process mode, and turns on the core's harness with it. The in-process mode has no settings of its own. The default subscription, each descriptor's settings, the retry cap and its dead-letter topic, and the payload limit are the broker's and the registration's. So a test runs the configuration production runs. It refuses what a server refuses, with the same error: a service URL the client cannot parse, a destination that is no topic name, a payload over the limit, and a handle used after shutdown. A second consumer of an Exclusive subscription is refused at once, where a server would keep it waiting. The mode keeps Pulsar's semantics: orders and persistent://public/default/orders are one topic. A message reaches every subscription over its topic once, and the subscription type picks the consumer within one. A negatively acknowledged delivery goes back to its subscription, and the dead-letter policy counts deliveries as the client does. A subscription starts at the end of its topics, and a seek moves it over the log the test published. A pattern reads a topic created later from the next listing, thirty seconds on. A header value that is not UTF-8 text fails the publish, as the client frames headers as text. A publish through the harness returns once every handler it woke has settled, a reply and a dead-letter move included. The assertions that follow read finished state. A delayed retry and a pattern's listing run on the runtime's clock, so tb.advance on a paused clock drives both. What only a server has is for a live test. Testing a Pulsar service tests a card payments service in process.

TestApp::start_live runs the same test body against a running Pulsar, for what only a server has. It connects the broker through its ordinary connect, so the client dials the server and every subscription opens a real consumer. The body is the one an in-process test runs; only the start call differs. A publish, settle and advance wait on the real clock until every subscription has handled what was published to it. The wait lasts ten seconds at most, and start_live_within sets another bound. The live mode is for what the in-process mode leaves to the server: the ack timeout's own redelivery; partitioned topics, and the partition a key picks; which consumer of a Shared or KeyShared subscription the server picks, and KeyShared hash ranges; messages published while a subscription has no consumer; a second Exclusive consumer waiting, and the OperationRetries that bound the wait; the token and TLS; a backlog older than the test, which start_at replays. A server keeps what earlier runs left in it, and a subscription is a durable cursor on it. So each run reads in a subscription of its own, which starts at the end of the topic, past what earlier runs published. In the example, stand returns the server's URL from PULSAR_TEST_URL, and the live test returns early without one, so cargo test passes on a machine with no server. A job that stood a server up sets RUSTSTREAM_REQUIRE_LIVE=1, and a missing URL then fails the test instead of skipping it. The repository's stand is docker-compose.test.yml, a Pulsar standalone on 127.0.0.1:6650 that just brokers-up starts. Testing a Pulsar service runs the same test against a server.

The two tests share one body: one in process, one against the server at PULSAR_TEST_URL. Он резервирует товар под заказы и записывает остатки по результатам сканирования на складах. Stock заменяет клиент сервиса остатков, и приложение открывает его при запуске.

A reservation left unsettled for a minute comes back. #[subscriber( PulsarSubscription::new("reservations", "inventory").ack_timeout(Duration::from_secs(60)) )] async fn reserve(reservation: &Reservation, State(stock): State<Arc<Stock>>) -> HandlerOutcome { match stock.reserve(reservation).await { Ok(()) => { tracing::info!(reservation.order, reservation.quantity, "stock reserved"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } // No answer: the subscription hands the reservation out again at once. Err(Refusal::Unavailable) => Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()), Err(Refusal::UnknownSku) => { tracing::warn!(reservation.order, "unknown SKU, reservation dropped"); Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()) } } } } Значение, которое возвращает reserve, решает, что происходит с сообщением в Pulsar: Исход В Pulsar ack сообщение подтверждается и больше не возвращается retry сообщение подтверждается отрицательно и сразу доставляется снова retry_after(delay) сообщение удерживается на время delay, затем подтверждается отрицательно drop сообщение подтверждается Сервис остатков, который не ответил, может ответить на следующий вызов, поэтому reserve повторяет. Сообщение возвращается в подписку, и на подписке Shared его может взять другой консьюмер. Артикул, которого нет ни у одного товара, так и останется неизвестным, поэтому reserve отбрасывает резервирование. В Pulsar нет команды, которая отвергает сообщение окончательно, поэтому drop подтверждает его, и сообщение исчезает. Сообщение, которое раз за разом не обрабатывается, покидает подписку через топик dead-letter. Клиент отправляет подтверждения в фоне. Завершение возвращает управление, когда подтверждение встало в очередь консьюмера, а брокер записывает его мгновением позже. Сервис, остановленный в этом промежутке, получит сообщение снова при следующем запуске, поэтому Pulsar доставляет каждое сообщение at-least-once. Обрабатывайте сообщение так, чтобы вторая доставка не навредила, например привязывайте работу к номеру заказа.

Доставка, которую никто не завершил, остаётся у своего консьюмера. ack_timeout в дескрипторе ограничивает её срок: когда срок истёк, клиент просит брокер доставить сообщение снова. Без тайм-аута такое сообщение возвращается, только когда его консьюмер отключается. Задайте тайм-аут больше самого долгого времени работы обработчика. Обработчик, который ещё работает, когда тайм-аут истёк, получит вторую доставку того же сообщения. Каждая повторная доставка засчитывается в предел повторов, как retry.

Подписка - это курсор, который хранит сервер, поэтому после перезапуска сервис продолжает с того места, где остановился. В ручной форме то же делает run_main. PulsarBroker::operation_retries client.consumer().with_topic(..).with_subscription(..) и цикл по консьюмеру обработчик #[subscriber] на PulsarSubscription .with_subscription_type(..) subscription_type в дескрипторе .with_topics([..]), .with_topic_regex(..) PulsarSubscription::topics, PulsarSubscription::pattern десериализация msg.payload.data тип параметра обработчика, который декодирует кодек consumer.ack(&msg), consumer.nack(&msg) исход обработчика (Подтверждение) .with_dead_letter_policy(..) max_attempts(n) и dead_letter(topic) в точке монтирования (Повторы и dead-letter) .with_unacked_message_resend_delay(..) ack_timeout в дескрипторе consumer.seek(..) start_at в точке монтирования или ручка перемотки в обработчике (Повторное чтение и перемотка) client.producer().with_topic(..).build() и send_non_blocking ответ или параметр Out, отправленный через политику публикации (Публикация и ответы) producer::Message { partition_key, properties, .. } шаг partition_key; заголовки становятся свойствами
Промышленный кластер требует TLS и аутентификации, а сервис решает, сколько ждать кластер и какого размера сообщения отправлять.

src/main.rs /// Where the cluster is and who the service is, as the deployment provides them. struct Cluster { url: String, token: String, } impl Cluster { fn from_env() -> Self { let read = |name: &str| env::var(name).unwrap_or_default(); Self { url: read("PULSAR_URL"), token: read("PULSAR_TOKEN"), } } } fn broker(cluster: Cluster) -> PulsarBroker { // Ten tries, three seconds apart; then the error. let retries = OperationRetries::attempts(nonzero!(10u32)).delay(Duration::from_secs(3)); PulsarBroker::new(cluster.url) .token(cluster.token) .operation_retries(retries) // The cluster runs with `maxMessageSize=10485760`. .max_message_size(nonzero!(10_485_760usize)) } Адрес подключения и токен развёртывание передаёт в переменных окружения. Клиент Pulsar подключается к одному адресу. К кластеру из нескольких брокеров ведёт одна точка входа перед ними: DNS-имя, балансировщик нагрузки или прокси Pulsar. Адрес pulsar+ssl:// ведёт к TLS-порту кластера, по соглашению это порт 6651. Клиент проверяет сертификат сервера по доверенным корневым сертификатам системы, а также его имя хоста. token выполняет аутентификацию по JWT, который клиент отправляет при подключении и при переподключении. Эту пару принимают и StreamNative Cloud, и собственный кластер с аутентификацией по токену.

Клиент сам переподключается после перезапуска брокера и повторяет любую операцию, которую кластер ещё не принял. По умолчанию он повторяет без ограничения, раз в пять секунд, и так пережидает перезапуск любой длительности. OperationRetries это ограничивает: десять попыток с интервалом три секунды, после чего операция возвращает ошибку с ответом кластера. Ограничение действует на поиск топиков, продюсеры и переподключение каждого консьюмера. Оно же превращает второго консьюмера подписки Exclusive в ошибку при запуске вместо ожидания. max_message_size - наибольшая полезная нагрузка публикации, по умолчанию пять мебибайт, как на сервере. Развёртывание, в котором изменён maxMessageSize сервера, задаёт здесь то же значение. Публикация большего размера возвращает ошибку в сервисе, не доходя до кластера.

Макросы Вручную src/main.rs #[subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("orders", "orders-svc"), reply)] async fn confirm(order: &Order) -> Confirmation { tracing::info!(order.id, "order confirmed"); Confirmation { id: order.id } } fn service(broker: PulsarBroker) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(confirm); }) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { service(broker(Cluster::from_env())) } src/main.rs struct Confirm; impl Handle<Order, Confirmation> for Confirm { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Confirmation, HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order confirmed"); ready(Ok(Confirmation { id: order.id })) } } fn service(broker: PulsarBroker) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include( subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("orders", "orders-svc"), Confirm) .reply() .build(), ); }) } fn app() -> RustStream { service(broker(Cluster::from_env())) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } Каждая настройка брокера - шаг билдера, который никуда не подключается, поэтому #[ruststream::app] строит приложение так же, как локально. Соединение открывается при запуске сервиса. Генерируемый документ AsyncAPI указывает хост и порт из адреса, но никогда не токен. Сервису, который перечитывает свои топики, нужна ещё политика хранения пространства имён на кластере.

Тесты запускают рабочий service с рабочим broker, которому передан тестовый токен, через TestApp::start. Pulsar внутри процесса проверяет адрес подключения так, как его разбирает клиент, но к кластеру не подключается. С адресом другой схемы запуск возвращает ошибку, и она называет схемы, по которым подключается клиент: the service URL's scheme "https" is not one the client dials: pulsar or pulsar+ssl TLS, токен и ограничение повторов действуют только на настоящем кластере.

Это руководство отвечает на сообщения Pulsar, публикует сообщения с ключом и заголовками через слот Out и публикует после запуска сервиса. Пример - сервис оформления заказов. Он подтверждает заказы квитанциями, отвечает на запросы цен, отправляет на склады листы комплектации и объявляет о себе при запуске.

Макросы Вручную src/main.rs /// The receipt of an order; the type names the topic it goes to. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "receipts")] struct Receipt { order: u64, } /// Confirms each order with a receipt. #[subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("orders", "receipts"), reply)] async fn confirm(order: &Order) -> Receipt { tracing::info!(order.id, "order confirmed"); Receipt { order: order.id } } src/main.rs /// The receipt of an order; the type names the topic it goes to. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[outgoing(name = "receipts")] struct Receipt { order: u64, } /// Confirms each order with a receipt. struct Confirm; impl Handle<Order, Receipt> for Confirm { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Receipt, HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order confirmed"); ready(Ok(Receipt { order: order.id })) } } confirm возвращает Receipt, и фреймворк его публикует. #[outgoing(name = "receipts")] закрепляет топик за типом, поэтому подписчику достаточно аргумента reply макроса без имени. В ручной форме - .reply(). Политика публикации брокера, Publish из прелюдии, используется по умолчанию, поэтому простой include отвечает через неё. Публикация возвращает управление, когда брокер сохранил сообщение.

Макросы Вручную src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize)] struct QuoteRequest { request: u64, items: u32, } /// A price quote; the mount site names where it goes. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] struct Quote { request: u64, total_cents: u64, } /// Answers a quote request on `quotes`, the topic the requesting services read. #[subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("quote-requests", "quotes"), reply("quotes"))] async fn quote(request: &QuoteRequest) -> Quote { Quote { request: request.request, total_cents: u64::from(request.items) * 1_250, } } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] struct QuoteRequest { request: u64, items: u32, } /// A price quote; the mount site names where it goes. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] struct Quote { request: u64, total_cents: u64, } /// Answers a quote request on `quotes`, the topic the requesting services read. struct AnswerQuote; impl Handle<QuoteRequest, Quote> for AnswerQuote { fn handle( &self, request: &QuoteRequest, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Quote, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(Quote { request: request.request, total_cents: u64::from(request.items) * 1_250, })) } } Quote не называет топик, поэтому его называет reply("quotes") в точке монтирования. В ручной форме - .reply().to("quotes"). Тогда тот же тип может отвечать в другой топик в другом сервисе. Запрос и ответ на него проходят через два обычных топика. Сервис, который запрашивает цены, публикует в quote-requests и читает quotes через собственную подписку. Он сопоставляет каждый ответ с запросом по общему для двух сообщений номеру request.
